item.title: China's major stock indexes surge, chip shares rally
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
BEIJING -- China's major stock indexes surged on Friday, with strong gains in sectors across the semiconductor supply chain. The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index reclaimed the 3,600-point mark, closing 3.73 percent higher to end the day at 3,606.49 points. The Shenzhen Component Index closed 7.24 percent higher at 10,814.02 points. The ChiNext Index, tracking China's Nasdaq-style board of growth enterprises, surged 11.61 percent, while the STAR Composite Index, which reflects the performance of stocks on China's sci-tech innovation board, jumped 14.21 percent. Semiconductor and electronics stocks led the rally, alongside electronic chemicals makers and stocks linked to China's national semiconductor fund. Shares tied to co-packaged optics (CPO) and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) also posted strong gains, while banking shares were among the laggards. A State Council executive meeting on Friday stressed that the capital market is vital to overall economic development, calling for efforts to strengthen counter-cyclical adjustments and tackle critical reform tasks at the same time. The meeting also pointed to the need to improve market-stabilizing mechanisms, give full play to existing policies, and mull and introduce new measures to promote steady and sound development of the capital market. According to the meeting, efforts should be made to encourage listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share repurchases, give greater play to state-backed funds in steadying the market, and optimize the quasi-"stabilization fund" function of the state-owned Central Huijin Investment Ltd. to provide sufficient liquidity. The meeting also underlined the need to improve policies to support and guide medium- and long-term funds such as insurance funds, enterprise annuities, and social security funds into the market, and strengthen the capacity to guard against and respond to imported risks.

item.title: The past, present and future of thrift shame in Europe
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
It was already 10 am, yet the winter sun at this latitude had not been up long enough to bring much warmth to the ground. In the lingering cold inherited from last night, about 20 people had gathered halfway along Rue Américaine in Brussels, their bluish cigarette smoke mingling with the white clouds of their breath, making the wait a little more bearable. Side A: An industry built on little things They were waiting at the gate of Les Petits Riens, which means "the little nothings", a well-known Belgian secondhand shop founded in 1937. It accepts donations from the public, sorts and refurbishes them, and sells them as secondhand goods to support charitable causes. For more than eight decades, it is precisely these little nothings, donated by generation after generation, that have kept the business going. According to figures released by Les Petits Riens, it received 8,867 metric tons of donated goods in 2025, equivalent to more than 24 tons every day. Previously published figures show that about 3.2 million secondhand items find new owners through its network annually. With the goods themselves coming from donations, prices can be brought down to levels affordable even to those on a tight budget. There are plenty of handbags in decent condition, sitting in compartments and priced at just one euro a piece, while even those hanging on display racks cost only a few euros or slightly more than 10 euros, roughly the price of one of the cheapest meal deals at McDonald's. Secondhand does not necessarily mean second-rate. Quite the contrary, in a society where donations are common and secondhand goods circulate efficiently, many everyday items enter the secondhand market long before they show serious signs of wear. Here you can find well-maintained sneakers that are by no means out of fashion; clean and tidy stuffed toys that look little different from brand-new ones; and even wooden decorations that might once have cost quite a bit, allowing those with limited budgets to add a little charm to their homes. On one shelf stood four decorative wooden letters spelling out "HOME" — Yes, in a European secondhand shop, you can even buy a "HOME". And behind that home lies an entire industry that creates a virtuous circle. First, the environment benefits. A stuffed toy sitting in the window of a secondhand shop certainly does more good for the environment than one lying in a garbage bin, covered in rotten vegetable leaves and leftover soup. Second, Europe's sizable low-income population stands to benefit. According to Eurostat, 72.4 million people, or 16.3 percent of the European Union population, were at risk of income poverty in 2025, meaning their equivalized disposable household income was below 60 percent of their national median. Figures released on Nov 17 further showed that about 28 million EU residents experienced severe material and social deprivation. Making desirable products affordable to those who are less well-off is a good move. On the other hand, a well-functioning secondhand market also allows people to donate or resell things they no longer need, perhaps recovering some of their money while freeing up precious space in their increasingly more expensive homes. Third, the industry creates jobs. Between being collected and appearing in a shop window, a secondhand item may go through sorting, cleaning, refurbishment, transportation and retailing, each of which creates jobs. A study by Oxford Economics found that the secondhand clothing sector alone directly supported about 110,000 jobs across the EU, generating approximately 3 billion euros in direct gross value added. As a comparison, the BMW Group employs about 107,000 people across Europe. In other words, the secondhand clothing sector alone supports more direct jobs than this global automotive giant employs in Europe. Add secondhand furniture, books and household goods, and one begins to appreciate how many livelihoods depend on this industry. Even I could not resist buying something during the visit: a secondhand tripod for five euros. I put it to use right there in the shop — just see how well it works! Side B: From thrift chic to thrift shame — and beyond Yet as Europe's economy struggles to regain momentum, buying secondhand has quietly taken on a different meaning. According to the European Commission's autumn economic forecast released on Nov 17, the EU's real GDP grew by 0.4 percent, 1.4 percent and 1.4 percent in 2023, 2024 and 2025 respectively, with growth projected at just 1.4 percent this year. Europe has thus spent nearly four years on a path of sluggish growth. However, EU inflation is projected to reach 3.3 percent this year. European Commission figures show that between 2015 and 2025, overall consumer prices rose by 32.9 percent, while food prices climbed by 48 percent and those of electricity, gas and other fuels by 62.7 percent. In 2025, about 34 million EU residents spent more than 40 percent of their household disposable income on housing. For an ordinary European, it's a major issue to count how much money is left in the wallet each month after paying the rent, settling the utility bills and buying groceries. That's also why so many Europeans have taken to the streets in protest this year — the people are angry and do you hear them sing? Against this backdrop, buying secondhand is becoming, for some Europeans, less a matter of environmental awareness than a practical response to the rising cost of living. Nora and Eve, a young couple I met in the shop, were browsing through handbags and clothes. "Because it's more ecological, and in this case, it's also a social project," Eve said when asked why she chose to shop secondhand. Nora added another consideration: "For me, it's ethical, and also because of the price." More than a decade ago, buying secondhand was promoted as something fashionable. In 2009, German supermodel Heidi Klum and British singer Sophie Ellis-Bextor helped promote secondhand clothing for the charity Oxfam. In 2012, British actress Joanna Lumley fronted a campaign encouraging clothing reuse and even worked behind the till of a secondhand shop the following year. The message was clear: Buying secondhand was not a sign of an empty wallet, but a statement of fashion, environmental awareness and social responsibility. As financial pressures mounted around 2020, however, another perception of secondhand shopping became apparent — the embarrassment associated with buying secondhand for fear of being seen as financially struggling. Or maybe we can call it "secondhand shame" or "thrift shame". The logic behind it is not difficult to understand: Those who can afford brand-new products can proudly tell their friends that they buy secondhand to protect the environment. Yet in comparison, those who buy secondhand because they cannot afford new products might find it a little harder to talk about that openly. Just imagine the dramaticness at seeing that new thrift shame fading only several years after it emerged. That's not because economy is turning better, but because it's getting worse, and financial difficulties have become a more widely shared experience. Gerrit Valere, an elderly gentleman I met in the shop, described this change in attitudes. A few years ago, he recalled, friends might have wondered whether someone visiting a secondhand shop was experiencing financial difficulties. Nowadays, with so many people turning up in secondhand shops themselves, there seems to be nothing unusual about it anymore. Valere showed us his secondhand treasures: a suit jacket, trousers and a padded vest, among other items. For just over 30 euros, he could maintain his gentlemanly appearance, and he seemed quite pleased with the bargain. It is good to see thrift shame fading. It's not good to see that financial pressure may be one of the reasons behind its disappearance. It was in 1937 that the Les Petits Riens was built, when World War II had already broken out in Asia and Europe was still living in the shadow of the Great Depression, on the eve of another devastating war. Built on public donations and dedicated to giving back to society, the secondhand shop had played its role well for decades, even through the postwar reconstruction days and turned into a sign of environmentalism. Its founders might not have thought that nearly 90 years later, amid another period of economic difficulty, it would once again become something people need lean on. It's not what they hope to see, either. What European countries need to do now is reinvigorate their economies, so that one day people can walk into secondhand shops because they want to protect the environment, rather than because they cannot afford to shop elsewhere. The ideal future of thrift shame is not simply one in which nobody feels ashamed of buying secondhand, but one in which everybody has the freedom to choose whether to buy secondhand. Perhaps only then will the original vision of the shop's founders be fully realized.

item.title: Mayors in global dialogue share experiences and outcomes
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
The 2026 Global Mayors Dialogue took place on Thursday in Urumqi, Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, bringing together mayors and other representatives from 26 cities across 13 countries to exchange views on modern urban governance concepts and share practical experience and outcomes. Themed "Putting People First, Driving Innovation: Working Together to Build Modern Cities for the People", the event drew more than 200 participants from countries including Chile, Georgia, Pakistan, Thailand and the United States. Attendees discussed effective measures to promote green and low-carbon development, encourage innovation and uphold "virtue and goodness". Samir Seyidahmadlil, deputy plenipotentiary representative of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan in Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, said the theme raises the practical question of how a modern city should improve people's lives — specifically measuring progress by how much easier, healthier and more secure people's lives become. He said better coordination, faster responses and good decisions based on reliable information can drive innovation and make public services more accessible. Cities can embrace green practices while remaining true to their history and can renew neighborhoods while preserving architectural identity and community life. Seyidahmadlil called for further exchanges and cooperation between cities in Azerbaijan and China in all these areas. Paul B. Thole, permanent secretary of Zambia's Eastern Province, said the theme speaks directly to the representatives' shared mission of ensuring that development improves people's lives. "Our cities may be geographically apart, but we are united in our faith in progress, innovation and excellence," he said, while also stressing the shared emphasis on collaboration. He added that Zambia's Eastern Province is a major food producer in the country, and agriculture remains the backbone of its economy and people's livelihoods. "We see great opportunities for a people-centered friendship in key areas such as agriculture," Thole said, referring to Xinjiang. Yakup Paydulla, mayor of Urumqi, the region's capital, said the city has leveraged opening-up as a significant advantage and opportunity in recent years. This has raised the level of opening-up in its pilot free trade zone, international land port area and comprehensive bonded zone, as well as driving a surge in both trade volume and international passenger numbers. It has built sister-city relationships with 39 cities in 27 countries. He said Urumqi will further expand trade exchanges and cooperation with foreign counterparts, continue to improve services for foreign nationals and strengthen international business and investment capacity. It will also regularly organize mutual visits, touring performances, youth exchange activities (such as summer camps and sports events), while building online exchange platforms. Ahead of the dialogue, the mayors and city representatives visited cities across Xinjiang, including Kashgar, Yining, Karamay and Kuqa and discussed related topics.

item.title: Doping control in sports made stricter
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
Individuals who repeatedly induce, instigate or deceive athletes into using performance-enhancing drugs for major domestic or international sports competitions will be considered criminals and could face up to three years in prison as well as fines, according to a new legal document. China's top judicial authorities — the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate — jointly issued a judicial interpretation on Thursday, clarifying what constitutes "severe circumstances" in doping-related criminal cases. The interpretation specifies that encouraging, persuading or deceiving child or disabled athletes into using performance-enhancing drugs also qualifies as a serious offense, beyond repeated offenses or targeting multiple athletes. Offenders in such cases could face up to three years in prison or detention, as well as fines. Other severe circumstances include repeat offenses within two years of being sanctioned or penalized for doping violations, causing significant harm to athletes' physical or mental health, obtaining illegal gains exceeding 50,000 yuan ($7,800), and engaging in activities with a serious negative social impact. The 14-article interpretation, which takes effect on Tuesday, aims to assist judges and prosecutors across China in effectively cracking down on doping-related criminal activities, thereby protecting the integrity of sports competitions and the well-being of athletes, the legal document said. "Defining these serious circumstances will eliminate confusion in legal practice and enhance the accuracy and efficiency of handling relevant cases," it said. The interpretation also highlights that doping-related criminal activities operate along a chain involving smuggling, illegal production, sale and use. It clearly states that smuggling substances listed in the doping catalog will be identified as a crime of smuggling goods and articles prohibited by the country from being imported or exported. Xu Hao, a lawyer at Beijing Jingsh Law Firm, said the judicial interpretation is significant for ensuring fairness and justice in sports as domestic and international sporting events become more frequent and diverse. "Strict doping control helps prevent fraud and other irregularities in sports competitions, maintains order and promotes the standardization of sports activities," he said. "It will also provide stronger protection for athletes' legitimate rights and interests." He underscored that strengthening the legal framework in the sports sector is also conducive to improving the country's image in sports governance under the rule of law. "Doping is a key issue in global sports governance. Regular enforcement of criminal law demonstrates China's firm determination to crack down on prohibited practices in sports, aligns with international sports rules and enhances the credibility and international image of China's sports industry," he added. China has consistently maintained a firm stance against doping, implementing various measures to establish an anti-doping environment in the sports industry. In July, the country unveiled a new five-year plan to promote sports development, outlining 38 key tasks covering areas such as mass fitness, elite sports, youth physical education and the anti-doping program. The Sports Law, which took effect in January 2023, added a dedicated chapter against doping. It explicitly prohibits doping in sports and states that no organization or individual may organize, force, deceive, instigate or entice athletes to indulge in doping, or provide or disguise the provision of doping. The law also clarifies the responsibilities of relevant government agencies and establishes an independent testing system, reflecting a "zero tolerance" stance against doping. It further supports public education, scientific research and promotion, and international cooperation, creating a relatively systematic legal framework for the prevention of doping. caoyin@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China opposes proposed US tariffs
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
China has voiced firm opposition to the United States' latest proposals to ratchet up tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, the Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday, urging Washington to "correct its wrongdoings" and resolve trade differences through dialogue and consultation. "The US Section 301 investigations are typical acts of unilateralism that seriously disrupt the international economic order and violate World Trade Organization rules," He Yadong, a spokesman for the ministry, said at a news conference in Beijing. On Wednesday, the Office of the US Trade Representative announced the findings of its investigations into the so-called "structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors" and proposed additional tariffs on imports from 14 economies, including China, the European Union and Japan, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. For China, the proposal accounts for the commitments and 20 percent tariff rate announced as part of the Kuala Lumpur joint arrangement, as well as certain existing Section 301 duties, the office said. The proposed measures remain subject to hearings and public comment before they can be finalized. However, the Office of the US Trade Representative said that it could consider tariffs of up to 40 percent on all Chinese goods if it determines that ongoing talks with Beijing have not adequately addressed the issues raised in the investigations. Responding to the proposed tariff hikes, the ministry spokesman said China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its legitimate rights and interests. The spokesman also noted that the US proposal includes exemptions for products on the $30 billion tariff reduction list, calling on Washington to expedite its internal procedures and work with Beijing to swiftly implement the agreed reciprocal tariff cuts. Cui Fan, a professor of international trade at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said that Washington is seeking to perpetuate its protectionist trade policies by reviving sweeping tariffs struck down by the US Supreme Court earlier this year. "The measures and tariff rates were broadly in line with industry expectations," Cui said. "The investigations merely pieced together a case to support predetermined conclusions." The National Foreign Trade Council, a US business association, warned that prolonged reliance on tariffs would also saddle US businesses and consumers with long-term costs while offering little prospect of resolving the root causes of "excess manufacturing capacity". "We are troubled by the administration's continued reliance on tariffs as the tool of choice to address complex international policy challenges," Tiffany Smith, the council's vice-president of global trade policy, said in a statement. That concern is shared by the American Soybean Association, which warned that the tariff proposals could expose billions of dollars in agricultural trade to retaliation. "Soybean farmers are barely more than breaking even this year after prior losses due to retaliatory tariffs," Scott Metzger, the association's president and an Ohio soybean farmer, said in a statement. Fresh retaliatory tariffs, he warned, could impose "a continued burden they cannot afford". Washington's tariff proposals came on the heels of the first meeting of the agricultural working group under the China-US Board of Trade in Beijing earlier this week, with the Commerce Ministry calling the exchanges "candid, in-depth and constructive". However, such unilateral moves are disrupting bilateral consultations and pushing other countries to take measures in response, said Zhou Mi, a senior researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation. "The two sides should focus on further tariff reductions and deliver on the consensus reached by the two heads of state to build a relationship of strategic stability," Zhou said. The two countries' economic and trade teams remain in close contact over a further extension of the Kuala Lumpur joint arrangement, He, the ministry spokesman, said at Thursday's news conference. The arrangement, reached last year, suspended the implementation of certain tariff and nontariff measures, and has since been extended to Jan 10. A further extension would offer businesses a relatively stable and predictable policy environment for cooperation and serve both countries' interests, He said. Rose Tu, Asia-Pacific vice-president of Americhem Inc, a US-based manufacturer of specialty plastic compounds and additives, said that its facility in Suzhou, East China's Jiangsu province, complements its manufacturing capabilities in the US and Denmark. "This collaboration allows us to bring together expertise and experience from different regions," Tu said. US aircraft engine maker GE Aerospace has also expanded cooperation with Chinese partners, signing more than $12.9 billion in sales and service agreements in Shanghai in early November. Xiang Weiming, its vice-president, said the company will continue to deepen its presence in China and provide reliable power for exchanges and cooperation between China and the world.

item.title: In search of Bruce Lee: Legacy beyond the screen
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
What makes Bruce Lee an icon whose influence still resonates more than five decades after his death? To mark the 86th anniversary of his birth, we revisit his legacy through the eyes of three people inspired by his life and philosophy. Joseph Clarke, an Irish Jeet Kune Do practitioner and young Sinologist who recently relocated to China; American filmmaker and kung fu expert Laurence Brahm; and Wang Zhipeng, chairman of the Beijing Wing Chun Martial Arts Association, share their insights into Lee's martial arts philosophy, his Wing Chun roots and the challenges he faced in Hollywood. From his famous "Be water" philosophy to his belief in breaking free from rigid styles, Lee championed adaptability, self-expression and constant self-discovery. Drawing on both Eastern and Western traditions, he used martial arts to challenge stereotypes and bridge cultures. His legacy lives on, inspiring new generations to think beyond convention and forge their own paths.

item.title: Belt and Road Documentary Forum bridges Xinjiang's perspectives to intl screens
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
A compelling story, interesting characters, and international coproductions that share perspectives, talent, costs and risks offer promising opportunities for documentary filmmaking, said Paul Lewis, special board adviser and international documentary consultant at the World Congress of Science and Factual Producers. Speaking at the inaugural Belt and Road Documentary Forum, held from Nov 11 to 13 in Urumqi, capital of the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, Lewis drew on his years of industry experience to encourage more productions showcasing the region and its people, technologies and green initiatives to global audiences. Hosted by Xinjiang Broadcasting and Television Station and the Belt and Road Initiative Documentary Consortium (BriDoc) initiated by the Communication University of China, the forum brought together more than 200 documentary producers and directors, decision-makers from broadcasting and streaming platforms, industry representatives and scholars from 18 countries and regions. It aimed to promote international coproduction, copyright trading and global distribution, while exploring market trends and fostering industry connections. Lewis, from Canada, said documentary filmmaking is expensive, labor-intensive and time-consuming, making it difficult for individual countries or organizations to shoulder the costs alone. "For many years, documentary makers have been going out and finding international partners. Now is the time for Xinjiang to become part of that process." He said Xinjiang's extraordinary landscapes, challenges and human stories offered great content for documentary storytelling. "It's a place where some of the most important questions about our relationship with nature are being confronted and answered every day. And the answers to these questions have the potential to inspire audiences far beyond Xinjiang and even far beyond China," he said, adding that the region's innovative solutions could offer lessons to other places. Lewis also stressed the importance of telling intimate personal stories with universal resonance and historical journeys that remain relevant today.

item.title: The world is watching Shenzhou XXIV
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has become the first foreign astronaut aboard China's Tiangong space station, where he will carry out experiments developed by scientists in Pakistan. The joint mission marks a milestone in China-Pakistan space cooperation and reflects China's openness to working with partners around the world on space exploration.

item.title: China develops Mandarin BCI for speech restoration
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
Chinese researchers have enabled a patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to communicate through thought alone, marking the country's first clinical trial of a wireless, invasive Mandarin brain-computer interface. Performed in September at Huashan Hospital Affiliated with Fudan University in Shanghai, the procedure involved implanting two 256-channel, minimally invasive electrode arrays into the brain of a patient surnamed Li. When Li forms words in her mind, the system captures neural signals from speech-related brain regions, decodes them via deep-learning algorithms, and translates them into both on-screen text and synthesized speech. For Li, whose ALS has left her barely able to move her lips, the technology has restored both her voice and her agency. "I have rekindled my hope for life," she communicated through the system, her words rendered in a vocal clone of her own voice. "The surgical trauma was minimal, recovery was quick, and I feel comfortable now." Li's descent into silence began in 2024 with tongue numbness, slurred speech, and arm weakness, culminating in an ALS diagnosis in 2025. As the disease progressed, even her husband could understand only about 20 percent of her attempts to speak. After more than a month of postoperative training, Li achieved encouraging results in spontaneous speech tests with theoretical coverage of the entire Chinese lexicon. During attempted speech, the system decodes more than 95 percent of characters in real time at roughly 80 characters per minute. During imagined speech, accuracy exceeds 90 percent at speeds of around 110 characters per minute — outpacing conventional assistive technologies such as scalp EEG or eye-tracking systems, which typically yield fewer than 40 characters per minute. "This first clinical trial has preliminarily verified the safety and effectiveness of the technology, which holds promise for millions of patients with speech impairments nationwide," said Mao Ying, head of Huashan Hospital. He added that the breakthrough not only offers new communication options for patients with dysarthria, but also charts a path toward a Mandarin-oriented BCI technical framework. The milestone represents a leap in overcoming the linguistic hurdles unique to Mandarin Chinese. Unlike English, which relies primarily on phoneme combinations, Mandarin is a tonal language. The syllable "ma", for instance, means "mother", "hemp", "horse" or "scold" depending entirely on pitch inflection. "In the past, international research on speech BCIs mainly focused on English," said Lu Junfeng, associate dean of Fudan University's Institute of Modern Languages and Linguistics and an associate chief physician at Huashan Hospital. "Because Mandarin has a unique tonal system and a vast number of homophones, we could not simply replicate foreign technical routes." To solve this, a multidisciplinary team from Fudan University, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, ShanghaiTech University, and Shanghai-based neurotech firm StairMed engineered a novel dual-target strategy. Using StairMed's wireless BCI system, surgeons implanted ultraflexible electrodes into two distinct brain regions, collecting 256 channels of neural data from each. One pathway isolates phoneme-related articulatory motor signals, while the other captures the tonal neural patterns essential to Mandarin comprehension. "Helping patients speak from their brains is not just about improving quality of life, but about restoring their right to equal expression, allowing them to be seen by the world and embraced by society, even while living with illness," said Lu. Zhang Menghan, dean of Fudan University's Institute of Modern Languages and Linguistics, noted that combining insights from clinical medicine and linguistics not only advances Chinese-language BCIs, but also opens new avenues for understanding the fundamental neural mechanisms of speech perception and production. The implications extend well beyond China. "Of the more than 7,000 languages spoken globally today, over half are tonal," said Li Yuanning, a researcher at ShanghaiTech University. "The technical route we have pioneered can also serve as an important reference for research into other tonal languages." Looking ahead, the team plans to refine decoding accuracy, enhance device portability, and expand clinical trials, with the goal of bringing the technology to more patients with speech impairments nationwide within the next two to three years. "Enabling patients to connect with the outside world through their own forms of expression is the ultimate goal of restoring language function," said Poo Mu-ming, a CAS academician and academic director of the Center for Excellence in Brain Science and Intelligence Technology. "In the future, this could pave the way for true human-machine integration."

item.title: Pakistani minister: China's space mission shows its inclusive approach
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-27
The successful launch of Shenzhou XXIV crewed spacecraft has captured global attention. Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has become the first foreign astronaut to visit China's space station. In an interview with China Daily, Pakistan's Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal said the mission demonstrates China's inclusive approach to development. By sharing advanced technologies, China can help improve people's lives across the Global South while paving the way for future international partnerships in space exploration. Watch the video!
